metadata.methods_description: Participants completed a resting-state recording of about 8 minutes (eyes open and closed periods of 63 s each), followed by four tasks in randomized order (words, faces, emotions, houses). Each task had a practice block and separate right-hand and left-hand response blocks (80 stimuli each, 160 total). Stimuli were shown for 1 s, followed by a fixation cross of 500-700 ms. Participants pressed the space bar only for target stimuli (animal names, female faces, houses with pitched roofs).

citation_details.title: Hemispheric segregation is evident in early perception, not just higher cognition
citation_details.author: Petunia Reinke, Sebastian Ocklenburg
citation_details.abstract: Introduction: Functional hemispheric segregation, the organization of distinct cognitive functions into separate hemispheres, has so far been investigated mainly using behavioral measures or fMRI. Whether such segregation manifests at early perceptual stages, however, remains unknown. The present study is the first to test Gerrits' segregation bias model using EEG, examining lateralization of early ERP components (N1/N170) across language, face, and emotional face processing. Methods: The present study is based on an openly available EEG dataset obtained from OpenNeuro. We analyzed data from left-, mixed-, and right-handed participants to investigate the influence of handedness and sex on early functional hemispheric segregation. Hemispheric lateralization was assessed using early event-related potential components (N1/N170) across language, face, and emotional face processing tasks.
